before: And it can't check its own work. Chapter Φ showed that no system can certify itself from inside, and psychology has the experiments to prove it for persons. People confidently explain their own choices with reasons that demonstrably weren't the cause.[^v1-c4-nisbett] In patients whose brain hemispheres have been surgically separated, the talking half cheerfully invents explanations for actions the other half initiated, and never notices it's guessing.[^v1-c4-interpreter] In "choice blindness" experiments, people shown a photograph they didn't choose, by sleight of hand, will often defend the choice they never made, with reasons.[^v1-c4-choiceblind] The self is something like a Gödel sentence: a statement about itself that the system can't fully verify from within. It can't be its own test set.
after: The trouble is that the brain's explanation of its work is another product of that work. Introspection can tell us what we seem to feel without reliably telling us how the feeling or decision was produced. People confidently explain choices with reasons that experiments suggest weren't their causes.[^v1-c4-nisbett] In some split-brain experiments, the speaking hemisphere supplies a plausible explanation for behavior prompted by information it did not receive.[^v1-c4-interpreter] In "choice blindness" experiments, people shown a photograph they didn't choose, by sleight of hand, will often defend the substituted choice, with reasons.[^v1-c4-choiceblind] None of this makes self-knowledge impossible. It makes the self's account evidence to examine, not a certificate it can issue to itself. In the language of our silicon mirror, training on your own answers is a poor way to build an independent test set.

before: When it closes, the self overfits. Interlude 2's model overfit by memorizing last year's exam; a closed self memorizes itself. The forms are many. Predictive-processing psychiatry now describes some of the rigidity of psychosis and depression as beliefs held too tightly against the evidence of the senses.[^v1-c4-rigid] Research on ideology finds that cognitive inflexibility, difficulty switching rules even in simple lab tasks, goes hand in hand with dogmatism and extremism, whatever the doctrine.[^v1-c4-zmigrod] Fundamentalism, religious or political, is the closed loop scaled up and given a uniform: a model that has stopped accepting new data, and calls that faithfulness. And at the far end lies a private world sealed against all correction, where nothing from outside can reach the story the self is telling itself. The monster within, I've come to think, isn't a separate creature. It's a loop that has shut.
after: When it closes, the self overfits. Interlude 2's model overfit by memorizing last year's exam; a closed self memorizes itself. Some predictive-processing accounts of psychosis examine how evidence and expectation receive the wrong relative weight, though the disturbance can differ across levels of processing; it is not simply believing everything too strongly.[^v1-c4-rigid] Research on extremist attitudes has also found associations with difficulty switching rules in laboratory tasks.[^v1-c4-zmigrod] Neither finding turns a metaphor into a diagnosis. But they give it something to work on: a person may become skilled at defending a story while losing the means to discover what the story excludes. The monster within, I've come to think, can grow in that protected space. Nothing gets in that might embarrass its landlord.

before: What keeps it open? Here the person has a power nothing lower on the ladder possesses. DNA's ripple can't choose its biosphere; the brain's ripple can't choose its body. But a person can choose the world it ripples through: new cities, new friends, new teachers, even a dormitory shaped like a beer can. Biologists call it niche construction when creatures reshape the environment that shapes them.[^v1-c4-niche] A person does it on purpose. Five centuries ago, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola imagined God telling Adam that every other creature had a fixed place, but he alone would have none, and must shape himself.[^v1-c4-pico] That's the Pinocchian bargain in its oldest form: to become a real person is to have no shelf, and to keep choosing where to stand. after: What keeps it open? A person can sometimes choose the world it ripples through: new cities, new friends, new teachers, even a dormitory shaped like a beer can. Other organisms also alter and select their surroundings; biologists call the feedback through environmental modification niche construction.[^v1-c4-niche] We add the unsettling possibility of doing it with an imagined future self in mind. Five centuries ago, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola imagined God telling Adam that, unlike other creatures, he had no fixed station and must shape himself.[^v1-c4-pico] That's the Pinocchian bargain: to become a real person is to have no guaranteed shelf, and to keep choosing where to stand. And Chapter 3's dream hypothesis offers an analogy. If strange dream experience helps prevent a brain from overfitting to its day, might a life of moves help prevent a person from overfitting to one place?

Here is the further wager. Perhaps a person changes most deeply not when a belief changes, but when the rule for admitting evidence changes: whose objection counts, what failure must be noticed, which encounter can no longer be dismissed. Could we distinguish a self that merely acquires new answers from one that changes what it permits to count as a question? And could a chosen environment help produce that second change without merely installing a different orthodoxy? Novelty alone will not do; a cult can offer an entirely new wardrobe. The test would be whether the person becomes more capable of correction, including correction of the new story. That remains a question to work on, not a theorem smuggled out of Chapter Φ.

before: The real plot twist arrived when machines finally let us watch. Magnetic resonance imaging gave us detailed pictures of the living brain's structure by the 1980s, and in the early 1990s functional MRI began showing which regions grew more active during a task, by tracking changes in blood oxygen.[^v1-c4-fmri] Suddenly, what had been metaphor became map: a flare in the visual cortex, a blush in the amygdala, a prefrontal region working harder when people suppressed the truth. Freud's couch had been upgraded to a control room. What the maps showed wasn't a tidy hierarchy but the layered coalition Chapter 3 described, now seen at work: old emotional circuits tugging against newer deliberation, habits running beneath plans, and a default mode network that stays busiest when we're doing nothing at all, forever rewriting the story of who we are.[^v1-c4-dmn]
after: The real plot twist arrived when machines finally let us watch. Magnetic resonance imaging gave us detailed pictures of the living brain's structure by the 1980s, and early functional MRI studies used changes in blood oxygenation to infer activity during a task.[^v1-c4-fmri] Freud's couch had been upgraded to a control room, though its screens measured a vascular response, not thoughts themselves. The maps revealed interacting networks, with emotion and deliberation woven through them rather than stacked as an old beast beneath a new accountant. Even the default mode network, relatively more active during many resting conditions than during demanding external tasks, was busy with forms of internally directed thought.[^v1-c4-dmn] Doing nothing, apparently, required personnel.

before: Strike one that resonates with something it shouldn't, and you get the uncanny familiarity of déjà vu.
after: That uncanny familiarity without a place to put it is also how déjà vu feels to me; the tuning fork is my description of the experience, not its established mechanism.

before: It turns out that my amateur introspection lands remarkably close to serious theory. Stephen Grossberg's adaptive resonance theory holds that recognition and recall happen when an expectation resonates with a stored pattern.[^v1-c4-art] John Hopfield's networks, which we met in the interludes, are memories you reach by content rather than address: give them a partial cue, and they settle into whichever stored pattern it resonates with. The hippocampus seems to do something similar, completing a whole memory from a fragment. And Endel Tulving showed that recall works best when the cue matches the conditions in which the memory was made, which is why the smell of brewing malt on I-94 can bring back a whole year.[^v1-c4-tulving] Even the failures fit. Overload a network like Hopfield's, and its stored patterns start blurring into one another, which is a plausible model for how memories can run together when a brain has fewer connections left to hold them apart.
after: My amateur introspection has relatives in serious theory, though they are doing different jobs. Stephen Grossberg's adaptive resonance theory describes a match between incoming patterns and learned expectations, helping a system learn new categories without endlessly overwriting old ones.[^v1-c4-art] John Hopfield's networks offer another mechanism: learned connections make certain patterns stable, so a partial cue can lead the network back toward a stored pattern. It can also settle into the wrong pattern, or a mixture never deliberately stored.[^v1-c4-hopfield] Hippocampal pattern completion gives biological support to the idea that a fragment can bring back linked parts of an episode.[^v1-c4-completion] And Endel Tulving and Donald Thomson's encoding-specificity principle explains why a cue's usefulness depends on how it relates to the original encoding.[^v1-c4-tulving] Brewing malt on I-94 does not contain my first year in Milwaukee. It has an excellent forwarding address.

before: There's one more consolation in this picture. Surgeons sometimes cool a patient's body until the brain's electrical activity falls silent and stop the circulation entirely, for as long as an hour, to operate on the heart or the great vessels. The patients wake with their memories and personalities intact.[^v1-c4-dhca] The hum carries the moment; the structure carries the person. The same connectome, meeting the same world again, strikes the same notes. That is why you're still you after a dreamless night.

But an answer arriving is not the same as an answer arriving with valid papers. Memory reconstructs; it does not simply replay. A familiar image may come from something witnessed, something read or something vividly imagined. Source monitoring is the work of judging where it came from, using contextual and sensory detail, traces of the mental operations involved, and what we know about the situation.[^v1-c4-source] Familiarity can arrive before that checking succeeds. The memory feels present; its passport is missing. Confidence is not a substitute for provenance.

Original conceptual schematic; the stages interact and are not a literal neural assembly line.](assets/04-chapter/memory-reconstruction.svg){#fig-v1-c4-memory-reconstruction width=100% fig-alt="A partial cue reaches overlapping memory traces. The tuning fork is alive, too. Synapses, cells and molecular processes must maintain the conditions under which a pattern can return; a wiring diagram alone leaves much out.[^v1-c4-maintenance] Yet a memory need not be continuously replayed to remain available. In a working-memory experiment, a temporarily unattended item became detectable again after magnetic stimulation, even when its active signature had dropped below the researchers' ability to decode it.[^v1-c4-latent] That is evidence about recoverability, not a brain switched off and restarted. Sleep is active, and surgical cooling is no proof that identity survives any interruption. I am tempted to call the living arrangement a *dynamic serialization*: the dance helps maintain the conditions for another dance. What must persist for that dance to remain mine is the harder question.

before: won not because it decoded the soul but because it outperformed everything else at predicting how humans behave in the wild.

before: Clinical psychology steps in when those patterns cross the boundary from quirky to can't-function, and in those extremes we glimpse truths that normality hides. Depression is not sadness; it's the gravitational collapse of motivation, reward and narrative. Anxiety is not fear; it's an ancient predator-avoidance system misrouted into a world where the predator is the inbox. Schizophrenia is not simply hallucination; it's the erosion of the membrane between thought and world, the inner narrator failing to tell self from signal. And in the spectrum conditions (autism, ADHD, bipolarity), the boundary between pathology and neurodiversity blurs. What one era calls disorder, another might call specialization. Half the Enlightenment might qualify as subclinical hypomania today. Half the tech industry certainly does. Somewhere, a monk and a clinician are disagreeing about whether a visionary is enlightened or in need of antipsychotics.
after: Clinical psychology steps in when patterns produce substantial distress or impairment; unusual is not by itself a diagnosis. Depression can collapse motivation and reward as well as mood. Anxiety can keep threat detection on duty long after the predator has become an inbox. Psychosis can disturb perception, belief and the sense of where experiences originate, though no single broken "self versus signal" switch explains schizophrenia. Autism and ADHD are neurodevelopmental conditions; bipolar disorder concerns, among other things, episodes of altered mood and energy. They do not form one interchangeable spectrum. The environment can make a difference to disability without making every difficulty an invention of social disapproval. Armchair diagnosis would give half the Enlightenment hypomania and half the tech industry a standing appointment. Somewhere, a monk and a clinician are disagreeing about whether a visionary is enlightened or needs help. Neither should diagnose him from the jacket copy.

before: Twin studies and large genome-wide studies remind us that the psychological deck is shuffled long before the first memory forms, though usually by thousands of genes with tiny effects rather than a few with large ones.
after: Large genetic studies find many contributing variants, generally with small effects, and some shared influences across psychiatric diagnoses.

before: But the environment still holds the pen: childhood stress, prenatal chemistry and the roulette wheel of lived experience carve the final contours. The genome is the blueprint; the world is the construction crew; chance is the foreman with a gambling problem.
after: Genes participate in development rather than supplying a finished blueprint. Childhood stress, prenatal conditions and lived experience interact with that inheritance. The construction crew works from instructions it keeps interpreting, while chance is the foreman with a gambling problem.

before: Libet's experiment, which arrived in the same season I did, was modest in method.
after: The experiment behind Libet's 1985 argument was modest in method.

before: The science has since added a twist worth knowing. In 2012, a team including Stanislas Dehaene showed that the readiness potential may not be a decision at all, but the brain's background noise slowly drifting toward a threshold; the movement happens when random fluctuations happen to cross it.[^v1-c4-schurger] On that reading, the early wave isn't the brain deciding for you; it's the brain idling until something tips it over. Deciding *when* to twitch a wrist was never the same as choosing a career or a partner. But the experiment hit a nerve because it cracked the story we tell ourselves: that somewhere in the control room, a little pilot labeled "me" pulls levers in real time.
after: The science has since added a twist worth knowing. Aaron Schurger, Jacobo Sitt and Stanislas Dehaene modeled spontaneous movement as noisy neural activity accumulating toward a threshold. Align many trials backward from the moment of movement and average them, and a readiness-like ramp appears; the ramp need not mark an earlier, completed decision.[^v1-c4-schurger] In a later experiment comparing arbitrary button choices with considered choices about donations, the familiar readiness potential appeared in the arbitrary condition but not in the same way in the deliberate one.[^v1-c4-maoz] Neither result proves free will. They do make the leap from choosing when to twitch to choosing a career look rather athletic.

before: Philosophers, confronted with this mess, did not all throw up their hands and go into accounting. Many reached for compatibilism: you don't need a magical exemption from physics to be free; you need your actions to flow from your own values, memories, character and deliberation, even if those were shaped by the past.[^v1-c4-dennett] Kahneman's two systems give the practical picture. Most of what we call will is System 1 firing first and System 2 writing a well-reasoned apology afterward. Free will, if it exists at all, may consist of editing impulses rather than generating them.
after: Philosophers, confronted with this mess, did not all throw up their hands and go into accounting. Many reached for compatibilism: you don't need a magical exemption from physics to be free; you need your actions to flow from your own values, memories, character and deliberation, even if those were shaped by the past.[^v1-c4-dennett] I don't believe in free will. But that does not oblige me to claim that the universe is demonstrably deterministic, or that deliberation does nothing. A reason heard, an imagined consequence or a conversation can change what the brain does next. Those causes do not become unreal because they operate through me. The person need not stand outside causation to participate in it.

before: Morality's favorite parlor trick shows the editing at work. A runaway trolley is heading for five people; pull a lever, and it kills one instead. Most people say yes; the numbers look clean. Now you must push a large man off a footbridge to stop the trolley. Suddenly the arm gets heavy. The math hasn't changed, but contact has, and brain scans show the emotional circuits weighing in far more heavily on the second version.[^v1-c4-trolley] Psychology quietly overrules philosophy. When those circuits are damaged, as in the famous case of Phineas Gage, the railroad foreman whose personality changed after an iron rod passed through his frontal lobe, the person doesn't lose a soul but loses filters. Impulse leaks where inhibition once lived.
after: Morality's favorite parlor trick exposes some of that participation. A runaway trolley is heading for five people; pull a lever, and it kills one instead. Many people say yes; the numbers look clean. Now you must push a large man off a footbridge to stop the trolley. Suddenly the arm gets heavy. The arithmetic survives, but the action changes: personal force, intention and using someone as a means affect judgment, not simply whether skin touches skin.[^v1-c4-trolley] The psychological machinery weighs features the head count misses. Damage can alter that weighing. Phineas Gage, the railroad foreman who survived an iron rod through his frontal lobes, became a famous case of changed behavior. His later ability to work also matters: the endlessly repeated story of a personality permanently demolished leaves out evidence of adaptation.[^v1-c4-gage] A person is injured in time, and may recover in time; neither the skull nor the anecdote should be treated as a sealed box.

before: Whatever will is, it's neither simple nor evenly distributed.
after: Whatever we call these capacities for control, they are neither simple nor evenly distributed.

before: So stop treating free will as a light switch and treat it as a dimmer. At one end sit reflexes and ingrained habits, with almost no conscious wiggle room; at the other, slow deliberation, imagining futures and overriding the first impulse. Most of life happens in between: messy, biased, influenceable, but not entirely scripted. Does believing in that elbow room matter? Early experiments suggested that people told free will is an illusion cheat more and help less, but larger attempts to repeat those studies have largely failed to find the effect.[^v1-c4-belief] What does seem robust is the experience itself. The brain predicts what the body is about to do; when the prediction matches, you get the smooth feeling of "I meant that," and when it doesn't, you feel the glitch: *I don't know what came over me*. The sense of authorship is a dashboard: not the engine, but a useful interface for steering. Rip it out, and you don't become more honest; you just stare at chaos.
after: The capacity for control, then, is more like a dimmer than a light switch. Habit, attention, fatigue, practice and the situation change what a person can inhibit or reconsider. That does not settle the metaphysics; it tells us where to look for useful leverage. Early experiments suggested that undermining belief in free will increased cheating, but larger replication attempts did not reliably reproduce that result.[^v1-c4-belief] The experience of agency is itself a construction: predictions about our actions, their observed effects and the surrounding context contribute to the feeling that "I did that."[^v1-c4-agency] A feeling of control can be mistaken. Actual control can also improve. Confusing the two would be an unfortunate way to demonstrate our mastery of the subject.

before: A line often credited to Viktor Frankl, though it appears nowhere in his writings, says that between stimulus and response there is a space.[^v1-c4-frankl] Whoever said it first, neuroscience has shown that space to be smaller and more precarious than we'd like. But it exists, and defending it, widening it through reflection and practice, may be the central moral act of being a person. In that space lives the monster within, and also the only thing that can tame it.

One way that improvement happens is through appraisal. An unanswered message can be read as rejection, distraction or a dead battery; the interpretation helps organize the emotion and the next action. Reappraisal changes the interpretation rather than merely hiding its expression. In James Gross's experiments with disturbing film, participants asked to reinterpret what they saw showed a different emotional and physiological response from those asked to suppress outward signs of feeling.[^v1-c4-reappraisal] Neither strategy is universally best. Sometimes the message really is rejection, and an endlessly charitable reinterpretation is just motivated reasoning in nicer clothes. The useful skill is to keep an interpretation revisable long enough to choose a response worth having.

A line often credited to Viktor Frankl, without a verified source in his writings, places a space between stimulus and response.[^v1-c4-frankl] It is a good image, not a measured gap in the neurons. Reflection, practice and help from outside can change the response that becomes possible. In that work lives the monster within, and some of what may tame it.

before: Now consider what happens when that integration fails. Jeffrey Dahmer, the Milwaukee killer, did things so grotesque that our first instinct is to file him under another species and move on. But in his interviews, he doesn't sound like a movie villain. He sounds flat, muted, mechanically articulate, a man reporting on himself as if from the outside. The psychiatrists who examined him described capacities that shouldn't coexist in one skull: careful planning and deception alongside profound deficits in empathy; obsessive, controlling fantasies; and an intellectual recognition that what he'd done was monstrous without much felt remorse. His jury rejected his plea of insanity: whatever was wrong, he knew what he was doing.[^v1-c4-dahmer] It wasn't a mind overcome by wild impulse. It was a mind in which the self that plans and the self that cares for others never properly met, a private world that had stopped admitting outside evidence. In Alice's terms, a loop that had sealed.
after: Now consider the limits of reading another person from the outside. Jeffrey Dahmer, the Milwaukee killer, did things so grotesque that our first instinct is to file him under another species and move on. In his interviews, his flat, mechanically articulate account of himself makes that filing harder. But a performance, even a confession, does not let us measure felt remorse. Experts disagreed at his trial; the jury rejected the insanity defense and found him legally responsible.[^v1-c4-dahmer] That verdict answered a legal question. It did not settle every question about his mind. Planning and concealment can coexist with appalling indifference to another person's life. Knowing how to manage people is not the same as caring what happens to them.

before: No single factor explains such a person: not genes, not early stress, not development, not a social world that missed the warning signs. Together they show a chilling possibility. The inner monster isn't an alien add-on. It's what can happen when ordinary psychological machinery develops under extraordinary, misaligned conditions. At one end of the spectrum is the person for whom regret is a regular, if annoying, visitor; at the other, the person in whom it never forms. Somewhere in the middle sits most of humanity, making small bargains with itself. Seen this way, the worst cases aren't monsters from another planet. They're catastrophic data points at the far edges of distributions that run through all of us.
after:
No single factor explains such a person: not genes, not early stress, not development, not a social world that missed warning signs. Nor does ordinary selfishness put someone on a conveyor belt toward murder. The disturbing continuity lies in shared human capacities, combined and developed in radically different ways, not a single scale with an absent-minded neighbor at one end and a serial killer at the other. Alice's sealed loop is one question to bring to the case, not its diagnosis. The worst cases still confront us with something difficult: they are human minds. Calling them another species lets our explanation leave the room before the victims do.

<!-- AI-assisted targeted addition, 2026-10-27: recovered punishment-as-pruning thread, kept at person level; for author revision. -->

It also changes the question we ask of punishment. If it is a kind of pruning, what are we trying to remove: a harmful action, a learned pattern, or the person who carries it? Restraint may be necessary to protect others. But suffering imposed is not, by itself, evidence that anything has been learned or repaired. The psychological question is whether the person can acquire a different response, under what conditions, and with what limits. The branch is not a bug in an otherwise innocent tree. We will come to the gardener later.

before: At street level, the moral mind doesn't look like a halo. It looks like a handful of very mortal brain regions arguing over how much to care. Regions such as the insula and the anterior cingulate cortex grow more active when we watch someone else in pain, as if the brain were running a small simulation: *what if that were my toe under the table leg?* Hence the involuntary wince when a stranger walks into a glass door. (Mirror neurons, cells in the monkey brain that fire both when an animal acts and when it watches the same act, were once hailed as the key to human empathy; the evidence for that larger role has since proved much thinner than the excitement.)[^v1-c4-mirror] But empathy alone doesn't make a moral agent; it just gives you shared flinching. To turn feeling-with into acting-for, the signal has to pass through the prefrontal cortex, the brain's diplomatic service, where "ouch" is negotiated into "don't" or "let's help."
after: At street level, the moral mind doesn't look like a halo. Parts of the anterior insula and cingulate cortex respond both to one's own pain and to cues that someone else is in pain, though the overlap does not mean we reproduce their whole experience. Hence the appeal of that little simulation: *what if that were my toe under the table leg?* Mirror neurons, first studied in macaque action and observation, do not by themselves explain human empathy.[^v1-c4-mirror] Feeling with someone, understanding their perspective and wanting to help them are distinguishable capacities.[^v1-c4-compassion] A skilled manipulator may understand you beautifully. A compassionate person may help without feeling your pain at full volume. No single prefrontal checkpoint stamps "ouch" into "ought."

before: Then come the chemical lobbyists. Oxytocin whispers, *trust them, they're one of us*, and, studies suggest, quietly favors the in-group over everyone else.[^v1-c4-oxytocin] Stress hormones dial up moral reactivity, so a traffic jam can feel like a betrayal of the social contract. Serotonin weighs in on fairness and impulse control, making sure you don't upend the Monopoly board every time you land on someone else's hotel.[^v1-c4-serotonin] Put together, you get not a single moral center but a parliament: regions, transmitters and networks lobbying over who deserves our care, when, and how much effort it's worth.
after:
Then come the chemical lobbyists, whose portfolios are less tidy than the popular press suggests. Some experiments administering oxytocin found increased favoritism toward an in-group, under particular social conditions; that is not a universal trust serum.[^v1-c4-oxytocin] In one study, lowering serotonin availability made people more likely to reject unfair offers without changing how unfair they judged them.[^v1-c4-serotonin] The reaction changed without the stated moral standard changing. Put together, we get interacting networks and bodily states influencing whose needs command attention and what we do about them. Chemistry enters the argument. It does not arrive carrying a pocket constitution.

<!-- AI-assisted targeted addition, 2026-10-27: recovered collective-superego thread, kept within personhood; for author revision. -->

And the witnesses need not be present. Parents, friends and teachers can remain as an internal audience long after we leave the room. The result is a kind of *collective superego*: a distributed conscience that feels private because we carry its voices inside us. We internalize the crowd's gaze, then call it "my values." That can help us keep a promise when nobody is watching, or keep an inherited prejudice when somebody finally is. Becoming a person includes learning which of those voices deserves to stay. The society that trained the choir will have its own chapter.

before: Our cousins run a proto-ethics lab of their own. In a famous experiment, Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal trained capuchin monkeys to trade a pebble for a slice of cucumber, which they happily accepted, until they saw a neighbor receive a grape for the same pebble. Then many refused the cucumber, and some threw it back at the experimenter.[^v1-c4-capuchin] A sense of unfairness, it seems, predates the courthouse by tens of millions of years. Chimpanzees and bonobos run coalitions, reconciliations after fights, sneak attacks and grooming trades; low-ranking males rise by political cunning instead of brute force.
after: Our cousins run a proto-ethics lab of their own. In a famous experiment, Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal trained capuchin monkeys to exchange a token for cucumber. They were more likely to refuse when a partner received a preferred grape.[^v1-c4-capuchin] The reaction was vivid; its interpretation was less settled. Was the monkey protesting unequal treatment, a disappointed expectation, or the experimenter who plainly had better produce? A later meta-analysis found no overall evidence for inequity aversion across the acceptance-and-refusal tasks it examined.[^v1-c4-inequity] That does not settle every question about animal fairness. It does warn against translating a flying cucumber straight into a declaration of rights. Chimpanzees and bonobos, meanwhile, reconcile, trade grooming and navigate alliances. The capacities from which our moral lives develop have a history longer than the courthouse.

before: And the monster isn't fixed, even in primates. Robert Sapolsky studied a troop of baboons for years, a hierarchy written in stress hormones and posture. Then the troop's most aggressive males died after eating tainted meat from a tourist lodge's garbage. The survivors built a calmer, more tolerant culture, and newcomers who joined the troop adopted it.[^v1-c4-forest] If baboons can rewrite their inner monster when the environment changes, the loop really can open.
after: And the monster isn't fixed, even in primates. Robert Sapolsky and Lisa Share described a baboon troop whose aggressive males were disproportionately lost in a tuberculosis outbreak linked to contaminated food. The survivors, now with a changed sex ratio as well as fewer aggressive males, showed a more tolerant social pattern; newcomers later participated in it.[^v1-c4-forest] This was an observed upheaval, not a randomized lesson in kindness. It nevertheless gave the idea of an unalterable baboon temperament a difficult afternoon. The environment a new male entered mattered.

before: Evolutionary psychology begins with an awkward confession: our minds were tuned for survival in small bands of hominins, not globalized nation-states with high-frequency trading. The circuits we use to navigate modern systems are older than agriculture, calibrated for face-to-face reputations, and easily hijacked by symbols that didn't exist on the savanna: money, brands, follower counts. We carry machinery for status, reciprocity, risk avoidance and coalition-building that once decided who got food, mates and allies. Today the same machinery decides who gets venture funding, who wins elections and who trends. The emotional infrastructure came long before the equations: the thrill of a win, the sting of a loss, the fear of being the sucker in a one-sided deal. (What happens when those ledgers are kept by markets is a later chapter's story.)
after: Evolutionary psychology begins with an awkward confession: capacities with deep histories are being asked to navigate circumstances they did not evolve specifically to handle. Reputation, reciprocity, status and coalition-building matter to a primate before they matter to a stock exchange. But the mind is not a sealed Pleistocene instruction manual. Development and culture alter what those capacities attend to and how they are expressed. A follower count can recruit an old appetite without being the same thing as rank in a small band. The emotional infrastructure comes before our formal ledgers: the thrill of a win, the sting of a loss, the fear of being the sucker in a one-sided deal. What happens when markets organize those feelings is a later chapter's story.

before: Layered on top of this ancient scaffolding sits something newer: epigenetic tuning. If genes are the rough draft, epigenetic marks are the margin notes written by life experience. They don't change the letters; they change which paragraphs get read aloud. In rats, the amount of licking and grooming a pup receives from its mother changes chemical marks on a stress-hormone gene, and with them how anxious the adult rat becomes.[^v1-c4-meaney] In humans, the evidence is harder to gather and more debated, but children raised amid chronic danger often carry nervous systems set to amber alert, quick to see threat and to grab now rather than wait, while children raised in stable networks of trust find it easier to wait, cooperate and believe that tomorrow will still exist.
after: Experience also reaches into gene regulation. Epigenetic mechanisms are not a recent add-on to biology; they help regulate which genetic instructions are used without changing the underlying sequence. In rats, differences in maternal licking and grooming were linked to chemical marks at a glucocorticoid-receptor gene, its expression, and the offspring's regulation of stress responses.[^v1-c4-meaney] That is more specific than life writing a personality into DNA. Human adversity can shape development through several interacting routes; the rat result does not establish that a person's later behavior has an epigenetic explanation. A nervous system adapted to danger may keep finding danger where a safer childhood would not. The adaptation can be understandable and costly at the same time.

before: When millions of individually tuned minds enter a marketplace or a voting booth, they don't leave their histories at the door. They bring them in as priors: embodied predictions about whether the world rewards patience, punishes trust or shrugs at fairness. In Alice's terms, every life arrives with its loop already partly set. So when we talk about rational actors, we're really talking about apes whose stress chemistry, attachments and cultural myths have pre-shaped what counts as rational in the first place. Psychology, in other words, isn't only about people on couches. It's about the inner chemistry that powers outer castles.
after: The person brings that history into the next encounter as expectations: whether patience is rewarded, whether trust is dangerous, whether tomorrow can be counted on. In Alice's terms, the loop is already partly set, but not finished. Psychology isn't only about people on couches. It is about how a world gets under the skin, and how a person then meets the next piece of world.
